summary: A 1971 proposal by Steve Crocker for a network standard format for a data stream controlling a graphics display. It was updated by RFC 125.

plainLanguage.summary: This 1971 proposal suggests one shared way to send drawing instructions across the network to a graphics screen. It is a starting point for discussion, not a finished standard.

questions: what was the network standard graphics data stream
what were the rfc 86 erase and replace commands
subtitle: A 1971 sketch of a standard stream of drawing commands for remote graphics displays.

tldr.problem: A user at a local console who works on a remote host needs the remote program's output drawn on a refresh display with point, vector and character capability, and each site would otherwise invent its own format.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal defines a display list and a screen, plus a stream of just two commands, Erase and Replace, that rebuild the lists a display controller executes.
tldr.outcome: The author calls the proposal illustrative only and a basis for discussion. It was updated by RFC 125.

today: The unit metadata gives RFC 86 the status Unknown, and lists RFC 125 as a later update. The text itself describes the proposal as illustrative and a basis for discussion.

sections.title: The Setup and the Model
sections.content:
In a typical arrangement a console is attached to a computer at the user's site while the user works on a remote host. The user's input goes to the remote host, and the host's output comes back to the local user. This proposal covers the form of that output stream when the console is a refresh display with point, vector and character drawing. The RFC names the DEC 338, DEC 340, IBM 2250 and IMLAC PDS-1 as devices in that class.

Steve Crocker states that the proposal is illustrative only and knowingly avoids important issues. Its main purpose is to give a basis for discussion. To define the meaning of the network standard graphics data stream (NGDS), he postulates a network standard display list (NGDL), a stream interpreter (NGSI), a list interpreter or display controller (NGLI), and a network standard screen (NGS).
sections.plainLanguage: A person types at a local screen but runs programs on a distant computer. This note proposes a common way for that computer to send drawing orders back to the screen.

sections.title: The Screen and the Display List
sections.content:
The NGS is square, with horizontal and vertical sides. A position on it is an ordered pair of unsigned 16-bit fractions: the horizontal distance from the left edge, then the vertical distance from the bottom edge. The resolution is deliberately left unspecified, so a picture should degrade gradually on lower-resolution displays.

Characters are assumed to be at most .015 screen width wide and .025 screen height high, which gives 67 characters to a line and 40 lines. The character set is ASCII, except for all form control characters, but the space character is included. Tab, return and line feed should be simulated by moving the beam.

The NGDL is a set of named, possibly empty lists. Names are 16-bit integers, and name zero is the chief list. Each item is one of five kinds: move the beam, display a vector, display the current point, display n characters, or execute another list with a given origin. The NGLI loops over the chief list forever, with origin always 0,0, and the last kind works like a subroutine call, so the interpreter is recursive.
sections.plainLanguage: The screen is a square sheet. The to-do list can say move the pen, draw a line, put a dot, write letters, or go run another small list and then come back.

sections.title: The Stream Commands
sections.content:
The NGSI parses the stream into commands in prefix form: an eight-bit operation code followed by any arguments. Each command is executed as soon as it is recognized. Only two commands are defined.

Erase consists of a single zero-valued opcode and no arguments. The NGSI makes all lists null, which erases the screen. Replace has an opcode of 1, a 16-bit list name, and an 8-bit subargument count, followed by that many subarguments. It deletes all items from the named list and rebuilds the list from the subarguments. There are five kinds of subargument, matching the five item types, coded as the 8-bit values 0 to 4.
sections.plainLanguage: There are only two orders. One wipes the whole screen. The other throws away one list and writes it again from scratch, item by item.
